subject: chemistry_2
question_text: How do you carry out the following conversions? i) N-ethylpropanamine to N,N-diethylpropanamine  ii) Aniline to benzenesulphonamide

verification.note: Unit 18 (Organic Compounds Containing Nitrogen) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.115-120, from the shaded sub-box "ORGANIC COMPOUNDS CONTAINING NITROGEN" of printed chapter 12 ("12. ORGANIC CHEMISTRY"); the book prints this question on book p.117 as SAQ 4. The 2+2 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK NAMING, corrected here: the printed question and answer call the product of part (ii) "benzene sulphonamide". The product from ANILINE and benzenesulphonyl chloride is N-phenylbenzenesulphonamide, C₆H₅SO₂NHC₆H₅ — benzenesulphonamide on its own, C₆H₅SO₂NH₂, would come from ammonia. This card writes the question in the book's words but names the product correctly in the answer and says so. BOOK STYLE: the printed answer puts "−HCl" over the arrow in both parts; the equations here carry HCl on the right instead, so that they balance as written.

steps.label: Adding the second ethyl group
lines: N-ethylpropanamine is a 2° amine and still
Heating it with chloroethane replaces that
hydrogen by a second ethyl group.
The HCl is taken up by an added base or by
steps.why: The reaction is a nucleophilic substitution: the nitrogen lone pair bonds to the carbon of chloroethane and the chloride leaves. Only the one remaining N–H hydrogen can be replaced, so a single step is enough and no further alkylation is asked for.
common_mistakes: Using ethanol or ethene as the reagent. An alkyl halide such as chloroethane is what supplies the ethyl group.
Writing the product as N,N,N-triethylpropanamine. Nitrogen already carries the propyl group, so it can take only two ethyl groups in all.
steps.memory_tip: Count the hydrogens left on nitrogen: one hydrogen means one more alkyl group can go on.
steps.margin_note: One balanced equation with a named reagent carries these two marks. Add that HCl is removed by a base.

steps.label: Aniline to the sulphonamide
lines: One hydrogen is left on the nitrogen, so
the product dissolves in aqueous KOH.
steps.why: Aniline is a primary amine, so one of its two N–H hydrogens is replaced by the sulphonyl group and one is left behind. That remaining hydrogen is made acidic by the strongly electron-withdrawing SO₂ group, which is why the product of a primary amine dissolves in alkali while the product of a secondary amine does not.
common_mistakes: Naming the product benzenesulphonamide. That name belongs to C₆H₅SO₂NH₂; the product from aniline carries a phenyl group on nitrogen.
Writing both N–H hydrogens as replaced. Only one is replaced, and the one left over is what makes the product soluble in alkali.
steps.memory_tip: Sulphonyl chloride plus a 1° amine: one hydrogen is replaced, one stays, and the one that stays is acidic.
steps.margin_note: Naming benzenesulphonyl chloride as Hinsberg's reagent is worth writing. The solubility line links this to the Hinsberg test question.

insider_note: Both parts are single-arrow conversions, so the marks are on the reagent and on the correct product. In part (ii) the product from aniline is N-phenylbenzenesulphonamide — the book's shorter name, benzenesulphonamide, describes the product from ammonia instead.
